report.summary: Reviewed chunk 5 of 5 of worktree.py: reap_branches and helpers implement fail-closed trust model; claims largely kept, one broken, several uncheckable.
risks: worktree.py:1121-1196 | medium | reap_branches docstring claims 'Every allocation is still examined first' but code stops examining after first failure? Actually no, failures are collected; but if _run_git raises for one allocation, that exception is caught and recorded, so loop continues. Need to verify that _run_git's RuntimeError is caught for rev-parse. Yes, it is caught. So claim kept. Risk is low, but the docstring's 'first one' wording could be misread.

worktree.py:1160-1163 | medium | _report_unverifiable_records returns rows with branch/path None; docstring says 'reported WITHOUT any field parsed out of the file' – the code does not parse fields, but the row includes branch/path as None, which is not parsed from file. Kept.

worktree.py:1200-1217 | medium | _refs_containing returns [] on failure, which retains branch; docstring claims 'A FAILED CALL IS NOT AN ANSWER' and 'Fail closed' – kept. But the comment about case-insensitive comparison says 'only effect of a spurious match is that a ref is dropped from the holder list, which retains the branch' – that is correct: dropping a holder makes the list shorter, possibly empty, leading to retention. Kept.

worktree.py:1219-1234 | medium | _delete_unused_branch uses -D after re-verifying tip; docstring claims 'the sha proof (re-taken here, so the branch cannot have moved in between) is what authorises -D' – the code re-takes tip and compares to proven_tip; if equal, forces delete. Kept.

worktree.py:1236-1255 | medium | commit_candidate docstring: 'The path is proven to be an allocated worktree first' – code calls _require_allocated_worktree. Kept. But docstring says 'a swapped directory would otherwise turn git add -A + git commit into a commit of the developer's working tree' – the proof is done, so that risk is mitigated. Uncheckable whether _require_allocated_worktree is robust.
worktree.py:1257-1264 | low | has_changes returns bool(self._run_git(...)) – if _run_git returns None on empty output? It returns string; empty string is falsy. Kept.

worktree.py:1121-1196 | medium | The docstring for reap_branches says 'a branch leaked by a CRASHED run is never reaped' – that is a consequence of the design, but the code does not explicitly handle crashed runs; it relies on _allocations being empty. Kept as a design statement.

worktree.py:1121-1196 | medium | The docstring says 'Records left on disk are reported as unverifiable and acted on by nobody.' – the code calls _report_unverifiable_records() and does not act on them. Kept.
worktree.py:1121-1196 | medium | The docstring says 'deleting the branch during cleanup would be wrong twice over' – this is a design rationale, not a claim about this method's behavior. Uncheckable.

handoff.purpose: Reap branch cleanup, allocation forgetting, unverifiable record reporting, ref containment check, force-delete helper, commit_candidate, has_changes.

symbols.name: reap_branches
symbols.note: Deletes branches only when both in-process allocation proof and git reachability proof hold; returns per-allocation report; raises RuntimeError on deletion failures.

symbols.name: _forget_allocation
symbols.note: Removes allocation from in-memory dict and discards on-disk record.

symbols.name: _report_unverifiable_records
symbols.note: Lists on-disk allocation records not vouched for by this process; never acts on them and never parses their fields.

symbols.name: _refs_containing
symbols.note: Returns refs other than the excluded branch whose history contains the given sha; fails closed (returns []) on git errors.

symbols.name: _delete_unused_branch
symbols.note: Deletes a branch with -d first, then -D only if the tip is re-verified to match the proven tip.

symbols.name: commit_candidate
symbols.note: Proves the path is an allocated worktree, then stages all changes and commits with optional author.

symbols.name: has_changes
symbols.note: Returns True if the allocated worktree has any changes per git status --porcelain.

claims.text: an overnight loop leaves one ref per attempt forever. That leak is real and this method closes it
claims.why: The method deletes branches that meet strict conditions, closing the leak for non-crashed runs; the docstring itself later admits crashed runs are never reaped.

claims.text: deleting the branch during cleanup would be wrong twice over
claims.why: The rationale refers to behavior in other modules (daedalus.spine.attempt, daedalus.kairos.shadow_shell) not present in this chunk.

claims.text: So reaping is a separate act, run by whoever knows the attempt is fully resolved.
claims.why: The method is separate from cleanup_worktree and is not called automatically; it only acts on allocations that have worktree_removed set.

claims.text: An earlier version enumerated <worktree_root>/.daedalus-alloc/*.json and believed what it read. That made the ATTACKER the author of the entire input set
claims.why: Historical claim about a previous version; not verifiable from current code.

claims.text: candidate code is handed its own worktree path, and the alloc directory is one .parent away from it.
claims.why: Depends on how worktree paths are allocated, which is in other chunks of this file.

claims.text: Two forged records naming real branches at their current tips were enough to delete feature/six-months-of-work and release-2.0, each with a printed reason that was false
claims.why: Historical attack description; not verifiable from current code.

claims.text: Candidate code runs as THIS user with THIS user's privileges, so there is no on-disk secret it cannot read and no on-disk file it cannot write.
claims.why: Threat model statement about the execution environment; not verifiable from this chunk.

claims.text: An authenticated record is therefore not available at this layer, and pretending otherwise would be the same defect with a MAC on it.
claims.why: Design rationale; not a checkable behavior.

claims.text: So a branch is deleted only when BOTH hold: 1. THIS manager object allocated it, in THIS process (:attr:_allocations, written by :meth:create_worktree), its worktree has been through :meth:cleanup_worktree, and its tip is byte-identical to the sha this manager itself read from git at allocation time. Nothing on disk contributes to this.
claims.why: The code checks allocation in self._allocations, requires allocation.get('worktree_removed') (set by cleanup_worktree), and compares tip to allocation.get('branch_tip_at_creation'). The on-disk record is not read; _report_unverifiable_records only lists them.

claims.text: 2. Some OTHER ref still contains that tip, so deleting the branch orphans no commit. This is git's answer, not ours
claims.why: The code calls _refs_containing(tip, excluding=branch) and only deletes if holders is non-empty. That function uses git for-each-ref --contains, which is git's answer.

claims.text: a candidate can only 'forge' it by genuinely making the branch redundant -- at which point deleting it destroys nothing
claims.why: If a candidate forces the tip to be contained in another ref, deleting the branch does not orphan commits; the code's condition holds.

claims.text: a branch leaked by a CRASHED run is never reaped, because the process that could vouch for it is gone.
claims.why: The method only examines self._allocations, which is in-memory; a crashed process loses it, so such branches are never considered for deletion.

claims.text: Records left on disk are reported as unverifiable and acted on by nobody.
claims.why: The code appends _report_unverifiable_records() to the report and never deletes or modifies those records.

claims.text: A leaked ref is cheap; a deleted branch is not.
claims.why: Cost/benefit statement, not a behavior.

claims.text: Returns: One dict per allocation examined, with branch, action (deleted / retained / absent / pending / unverifiable) and reason.
claims.why: The code builds a dict for each allocation with branch, path, action, reason. Actions include 'deleted', 'retained', 'absent', 'pending', and 'unverifiable' (via _report_unverifiable_records).

claims.text: Raises: RuntimeError: If any branch that was cleared for deletion could not be deleted. Every allocation is still examined first; the failures are reported together rather than aborting on the first one.
claims.why: The loop continues after a deletion failure (catches RuntimeError, appends to failures, continues). After the loop, if failures is non-empty, raises RuntimeError with all failures joined.

claims.text: The ref is already gone; the allocation has nothing to guard.
claims.why: When rev-parse fails, the branch does not exist, so the allocation is forgotten and reported as absent.

claims.text: branch tip {tip} is not the allocation tip {expected}: it holds commits this manager did not create, and deleting it would destroy work
claims.why: The code retains the branch whenever tip != expected, which is the stated reason.

claims.text: no other ref contains {tip}, so deleting {branch} would orphan it and the commits behind it
claims.why: The code retains the branch when _refs_containing returns empty.

claims.text: tip is unchanged since allocation and is still reachable from {holders[0]}; no work is lost
claims.why: The code deletes the branch only when tip == expected and holders is non-empty, so the reason is accurate.

claims.text: Name the on-disk records nobody vouched for. Never acts on them.
claims.why: The method returns a list of rows with action 'unverifiable' and does not modify any files.

claims.text: Reported rather than ignored so the leak is visible; reported WITHOUT any field parsed out of the file, because every byte in it is candidate-writable and echoing a forged branch name back at an operator as though it meant something is how the previous version printed false reasons.
claims.why: The code sets branch and path to None and only includes the file name, without reading the file's contents.

claims.text: Refs OTHER than refs/heads/<excluding> whose history holds sha.
claims.why: The code runs for-each-ref --contains sha and filters out the excluded ref case-insensitively.

claims.text: The one input to the reap decision that no candidate can forge.
claims.why: Depends on git's behavior and the candidate's inability to forge git's object graph; not verifiable from this chunk.

claims.text: If this is non-empty, deleting the branch cannot orphan a commit -- every commit on it stays reachable from something else.
claims.why: If any other ref contains the tip, that ref's history includes the tip and all ancestors, so no commit is orphaned.

claims.text: If it is empty the branch is the only thing holding that history, and holding history is exactly what this method must never destroy.
claims.why: The method retains the branch when holders is empty, so it does not destroy history.

claims.text: A FAILED CALL IS NOT AN ANSWER. git being missing, the repository being locked, .git being written by something else, a candidate that exhausted the handle table -- none of those is evidence that the tip is held elsewhere, so none of them may license a delete.
claims.why: The except clause catches RuntimeError and returns [] (empty list), which causes the branch to be retained, not deleted.

claims.text: Deleting the except below lets the RuntimeError escape reap_branches instead of retaining; that mutation SURVIVED the suite until 2026-07-28, and it is killed now by test_reap_retains_a_branch_when_git_cannot_say_who_contains_its_tip.
claims.why: Historical and test-related claim; the current code has the except returning [], but the test is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Compared case-INSENSITIVELY although git refs are case-sensitive: the only effect of a spurious match is that a ref is dropped from the holder list, which retains the branch. Erring toward retention is the correct direction for a method whose failure mode is deleting work.
claims.why: The code uses casefold() for comparison; a spurious match removes a ref from the holder list, making the list shorter and possibly empty, which leads to retention. This is fail-safe.

claims.text: Delete a branch already PROVEN to hold nothing but its base commit.
claims.why: The method is called only after the tip is proven to be contained in another ref, so the branch holds no unique commits.

claims.text: -d is tried first so git's own merged-check applies.
claims.why: The code calls _run_git('branch', '-d', branch) first.

claims.text: If git refuses anyway -- it compares against the current HEAD, which may have moved somewhere unrelated -- the sha proof (re-taken here, so the branch cannot have moved in between) is what authorises -D.
claims.why: The code catches RuntimeError from -d, then re-runs rev-parse and compares to proven_tip; if equal, runs -D.

claims.text: The force flag is never reached without that proof.
claims.why: If tip != proven_tip, a RuntimeError is raised before reaching -D.

claims.text: The path is proven to be an allocated worktree first: a swapped directory would otherwise turn git add -A + git commit into a commit of the developer's working tree.
claims.why: The code calls _require_allocated_worktree(path) before running git add and commit.

claims.text: Return whether the candidate worktree differs from its HEAD.
claims.why: The code runs git status --porcelain and returns bool of the output; non-empty output means changes exist.

observations.what: reap_branches docstring says 'Every allocation is still examined first; the failures are reported together rather than aborting on the first one.' The loop does catch RuntimeError for deletion failures and continues, but it also catches RuntimeError for rev-parse and continues. So all allocations are examined.

_report_unverifiable_records returns rows with branch/path None; docstring says 'reported WITHOUT any field parsed out of the file'. The code does not read the file contents, but it does include the file name as 'record'. That is metadata, not parsed content.

_refs_containing filters the excluded ref case-insensitively; the comment says this errs toward retention. If a spurious match removes a ref from the holder list, the list could become empty, causing retention. Correct.

commit_candidate uses _run_git('add', '-A', cwd=target) and _run_git(*commit_args, cwd=target). The docstring says the path is proven to be an allocated worktree first, which is done. The risk of committing the developer's working tree is mitigated if _require_allocated_worktree is robust.
has_changes returns bool(self._run_git(...)). If _run_git returns None on some error, bool(None) is False, which could incorrectly report no changes. But _run_git likely raises on error.
